cards.f: Four ways to measure business size
cards.b: Number of employees, value of output (revenue), capital employed, market share. Profit is NOT a measure of size.
Business sales ÷ total market sales × 100. E.g. €45m in a €300m market = 15%.
The total value of all long-term finance invested in the business.
Expanding the existing business (new branches, products, markets). Slower but less risky; the owners keep control.
Merger: two businesses agree to join and form one. Takeover: one business buys a controlling share of another.
Merging with a business in the same industry at the same stage of production (e.g. two hotel chains). Removes a competitor.
Backward: with a supplier (earlier stage). Forward: with a customer/retailer (later stage).
Joining businesses in unrelated industries. Main benefit: diversification spreads risk.
Average costs rise as a business grows too big: poor communication, lack of employee commitment, weak coordination.
Type of industry (e.g. personal services), small/niche market, owner's objectives (control, less stress), lack of finance.
Poor management or planning, over-expansion, poor cash flow, new competitors, changing tastes, recession. Lack of cash is common.
Social, environmental and financial objectives. Profits are reinvested to achieve the social aim.
Any person or group with a direct interest in the performance and activities of a business.
Owners want higher profit and cut wages, which conflicts with workers' job security; expanding a factory creates jobs but residents face noise and traffic.
Jobs and training, tax revenue, investment and technology, better balance of trade. Drawbacks: profits sent abroad, local firms hurt, pollution.

short.q: Explain why profit is not a good measure of the size of a business. [2]
short.model: A small business can make a high profit while a large one makes a loss, so profit does not show how big the business is.
points: small firm can have high profit
large firm can make a loss

short.q: Calculate the market share of a firm with sales of $18 million in a market worth $120 million. [2]
Explain two reasons why an owner may want the business to grow. [4]
short.model: Growth can bring economies of scale, which lower average costs and raise profit. It can also increase market share and status.
points: economies of scale / lower average costs
development of one chain of reasoning

short.q: Explain two problems a business might face after a merger. [4]
short.model: Different business cultures can clash, lowering morale and productivity. Job losses and poor communication across a larger organisation can cause diseconomies of scale.

short.q: Explain two possible benefits and two possible drawbacks of a multinational opening a factory in a developing country. [4]
short.model: Benefits: jobs and training, plus tax revenue for government. Drawbacks: profits are sent back to the home country and local firms may be forced out of business.
